newsitem.title: INDIA: Calcutta priest denies he said Mother Teresa is dying.
newsitem.headline: Calcutta priest denies he said Mother Teresa is dying.

text.p: A Jesuit priest who has acted as a spiritual adviser to Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity on Sunday denied saying that the ailing nun was close to death.

Referring to news reports that quoted him as saying Mother Teresa was dying, Father Edward Le Joly told Reuters: "I did not say she is dying. No, I never said that. What I said was that her condition is not really good. She has been suffering a lot."

The 87-year-old Jesuit priest who lives on the campus of Calcutta's St. Xavier's College added: "I haven't seen her for quite some time. I spoke to someone at the Missionaries of Charity and I was told that she was on oxygen three days back to help her breathing. She is certainly eager to see her successor who is going to be elected on February 2."

Mother Teresa, who has led the order since she set it up in 1948, has decided to retire as its superior general because of heart, kidney and lung problems which have forced her into emergency hospital care three times since last August.
The 86-year-old nun is now secluded at the Missionaries of Charity headquarters, Mother House, in central Calcutta.

Sister Marinetta, a nun at the headquarters, told Reuters by telephone that Mother Teresa's condition was "unchanged". She said the senior nun has back pain and is sometimes administered oxygen to help her breathe but there had been no sharp deterioration in her condition.
More than 100 nuns began a two-week retreat on January 16 to select a successor to Mother Teresa. The secret ballot has been set for February 2, Roman Catholic church officials said.
The 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner, known affectionately simply as "Mother", wanted to step down in 1990, one year after she was fitted with a heart pacemaker, but was persuaded to stay on.
The order's electoral college, or General Chapter, comprises representatives from various sections of its 4,500 nuns.
Set to end on January 31, the retreat was to be followed by several meetings of the General Chapter before the February 2 election.
